question_text: Evaluate ∫ √sinx/(√sinx + √cosx) dx from π/6 to π/3.

mark_split.label: Apply the property with a + b = π/2

insider_note: The limits π/6 and π/3 add up to π/2, exactly the angle where sinx and cosx swap under the property — that sum, not 0-to-π/2 itself, is what makes the swap trick work here.

steps.label: Apply the property with a + b = π/2
steps.margin_note: One mark. Use the general ∫ₐᵇ form here, not the 0-to-a special case — the limits are not 0 and π/2.
steps.memory_tip: π/6 + π/3 = π/2 — check this sum first, it is what makes the sin↔cos swap appear.
lines: We know ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x)dx
steps.why: The general King's property replaces x by (the sum of the two limits, minus x); here π/6 + π/3 = π/2, so the replacement is x → π/2 − x, the same swap that makes sinx and cosx exchange places.
common_mistakes: Using the 0-to-a special case of the property when the lower limit is not 0.
Computing a + b as π/6 × π/3 instead of the sum π/6 + π/3.

steps.label: Write the second form
steps.margin_note: One more mark. √sinx becomes √cosx under the swap.
steps.why: Since π/6 + π/3 = π/2, the swap x → π/2 − x turns sinx into cosx and vice versa, so the numerator and denominator terms exchange places while the limits stay the same.
common_mistakes: Leaving the numerator unchanged at √sinx instead of turning it into √cosx.
Forgetting that the limits π/6 and π/3 stay exactly as they were — only the integrand changes.

steps.label: Add and solve
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. The added numerator equals the denominator, so the fraction is 1.
steps.memory_tip: π/3 minus π/6 is π/6 — the length of the original interval survives into the final answer.
